title: Counting Important Terms · Level 2
slo: Explain how frequency analysis and TF-IDF identify document topics.

exercises.question_text: In the IDF formula, what is df(t)?

options.rationale: df(t) is the number of items containing term t. It is used with N in log(N/df(t)).

options.text: Uses of term t in one document
options.rationale: Uses in one item are TF. df(t) counts how many items contain the term.

feedback.intrinsic: You would put a local count into a collection-wide calculation.
feedback.instructional: df(t) counts items containing t, while TF counts uses within one item.

options.rationale: IDF does not count the tokens inside a term. It uses the number of items containing that term.
options.better_fit: This does not fit the IDF formula.

feedback.intrinsic: The rarity calculation would not reflect how widely the term appears.
feedback.instructional: For IDF, count the items that contain the term, not the tokens in its spelling.

options.rationale: Similarity scores compare vectors. df(t) is a count of items containing a term.
options.better_fit: Choose this when comparing semantic vectors.

feedback.intrinsic: You would replace a count with an unrelated comparison value.
feedback.instructional: IDF uses counts of items, not vector similarity.

exercises.explanation: Correct. df(t) is the number of items that contain the term.

exercises.question_text: TF-IDF gives low discriminative weight to a term that appears in every document.

feedback_for_incorrect.intrinsic: A shared term would be treated as if it separated individual topics.
feedback_for_incorrect.instructional: When a term appears in every item, its IDF is zero, so it contributes no distinguishing TF-IDF weight.

exercises.explanation: Correct. A term in every item has IDF of zero and no discriminative TF-IDF weight.

exercises.question_text: Which statements describe Term Frequency (TF)? Select all that apply.

options.text: It counts a term in one document
options.rationale: This is the definition of TF. It is a within-item count.
TF equals the number of appearances. Six appearances therefore give 6.
TF is multiplied by IDF to calculate TF-IDF. It is one component of the score.

options.text: It measures documents containing a term
options.rationale: The number of items containing a term is df(t). TF counts appearances in one item.
options.better_fit: Choose this when defining df(t) in the IDF formula.

feedback.intrinsic: You would use a collection count where an item count is needed.
feedback.instructional: Keep the scopes separate: TF is within one item, while df(t) counts items containing a term.

exercises.explanation: Correct. TF is a within-item count and one part of TF-IDF.

exercises.question_text: Arrange the following steps to calculate TF-IDF.

feedback_for_incorrect.intrinsic: The calculation would not produce the intended combined score.
feedback_for_incorrect.instructional: Calculate the two inputs first, multiply them, and then identify the result as TF-IDF.

exercises.correct_answer: Calculate TF Calculate IDF Multiply TF by IDF Get the TF-IDF score
exercises.explanation: TF and IDF must be available before they can be multiplied. Their product is the final relevance score.

exercises.question_text: The measure that checks whether a term is rare or common across documents is ___.

parts.text: The measure that checks whether a term is rare or common across documents is

feedback_for_incorrect.intrinsic: The label would point to a different kind of count or score.
feedback_for_incorrect.instructional: Use IDF for collection-wide rarity. Frequency analysis and TF count occurrences; TF-IDF combines TF and IDF.

exercises.explanation: This measure compares the number of items containing a term with the total collection size. TF counts within one item, and TF-IDF combines TF with IDF.

exercises.question_text: A support analyst has a large collection of support tickets. One ticket repeatedly mentions a term that is unusual in the rest of the collection. Which score should the analyst use to find that term?

options.rationale: The term is frequent in one ticket and rare elsewhere. TF-IDF combines both facts into one score.
Raw frequency counts appearances but does not account for rarity across the collection. It may elevate widely shared terms.
options.better_fit: Choose this for a quick topic clue from one item.

feedback.intrinsic: You might highlight a common term rather than a distinctive one.
feedback.instructional: Use TF-IDF when both repeated use in one item and rarity across the collection matter.

options.rationale: TF captures repeated use in the ticket. It does not measure whether the term is unusual elsewhere.
options.better_fit: Choose this when only the count within one ticket is needed.

feedback.intrinsic: You would miss whether the term is common across the rest of the collection.
feedback.instructional: TF is one input; TF-IDF adds IDF to account for rarity.

options.rationale: IDF captures rarity across the collection. It does not show whether the term is repeated in this ticket.
options.better_fit: Choose this when measuring collection-wide rarity alone.

feedback.intrinsic: You would miss whether the rare term is important in this ticket.
feedback.instructional: TF-IDF needs both within-item frequency and collection-wide rarity.

exercises.explanation: Correct. TF-IDF rewards a term that is frequent here and relatively rare elsewhere.

exercises.question_text: If “agent” appears six times in one document, its ___ is 6.

parts.text: If “agent” appears six times in one document, its

feedback_for_incorrect.intrinsic: The six-count result would be given the wrong name.
feedback_for_incorrect.instructional: Use TF for an appearance count in one item, not IDF or the combined TF-IDF score.

exercises.explanation: The measure is based only on the number of appearances in one item. IDF uses the collection, while TF-IDF combines two values.

exercises.question_text: Arrange the parts to form the correct statement.

feedback_for_incorrect.intrinsic: The comparison claim would be unclear to a colleague.
feedback_for_incorrect.instructional: Place the shared terms first, followed by what they cannot do, then the two items being compared.

exercises.correct_answer: Terms common in many documents do not distinguish one document from another
exercises.explanation: The sentence first identifies the shared terms, then explains their limitation: they cannot separate individual topics.

exercises.question_text: An analyst compares the Copilot Studio and Microsoft Foundry articles. Which terms have IDF of zero because both articles contain them? Select all that apply.

options.rationale: This term occurs in both of the two samples. Its IDF is log(2/2), which is zero.
This term is in both samples. Therefore its IDF is zero.
Both samples contain agent. A term present in every item has zero IDF.

options.error_type: Confuses a document-specific term with a term in every document
options.rationale: Copilot is specific to the Copilot Studio sample. It is not present in both samples.
options.better_fit: Choose this as a term with distinguishing value for the Copilot Studio topic.

feedback.intrinsic: You would treat a distinguishing term as if it were shared.
feedback.instructional: Only terms present in every item have IDF of zero in this two-item comparison.

exercises.explanation: Correct. Each selected term occurs in both items, so its IDF is zero.

exercises.question_text: Counting occurrences of normalized tokens to infer a document's topic is ___.

parts.text: Counting occurrences of normalized tokens to infer a document's topic is

feedback_for_incorrect.intrinsic: The chosen label would make the counting task unclear.
feedback_for_incorrect.instructional: Use frequency analysis for overall normalized-token counts. TF is one count, IDF measures rarity, and TF-IDF combines both.

exercises.explanation: This method uses normalized token counts to indicate a subject. TF, IDF, and TF-IDF measure narrower or combined aspects.

exercises.question_text: A content analyst compares a Copilot Studio article with a Microsoft Foundry article. Which terms would best help identify their different topics? Select all that apply.

options.rationale: Copilot is specific to one sample. It helps separate that topic from the Foundry sample.
Declarative identifies the configured-not-programmed approach. It is specific enough to distinguish the topic.
Foundry identifies the code-based development sample. It helps distinguish the two focuses.
Agent appears frequently in both samples. It identifies their shared theme, not their difference.
options.better_fit: Choose this when stating the broad theme common to both articles.

feedback.intrinsic: You would label both articles similarly instead of separating their focuses.
feedback.instructional: Use terms that occur in one topic, not shared terms such as agent, to distinguish items.

exercises.explanation: Correct. These terms identify the separate topics more clearly than shared terms do.

exercises.question_text: A support analyst has one long customer-feedback report and needs a quick clue to its main topic. Which method should the analyst choose?

options.rationale: For one report, frequent normalized terms can suggest the main topic. This is frequency analysis.
The situation has one report, not a collection comparison. Rarity across items is the role of IDF.
options.better_fit: Choose this when a collection contains many items with shared terms.

feedback.intrinsic: You would spend effort comparing items that are not part of the task.
feedback.instructional: For one report, count normalized terms. Compare rarity only across a collection.

options.rationale: Graph-linked sentence ranking is TextRank. It is used to select representative sentences for a summary.
options.better_fit: Choose this when selecting sentences for an extractive summary.

feedback.intrinsic: You would produce summary candidates instead of a quick topic clue.
feedback.instructional: Topic clues from one report come from frequent normalized terms.

options.error_type: Confuses frequency analysis with semantic similarity
options.rationale: Vector orientations compare semantic similarity. They are not required for basic frequency counts.
options.better_fit: Choose this when finding semantically related terms.

feedback.intrinsic: You would compare meanings instead of using the available counts.
feedback.instructional: Frequency analysis is the direct method when the goal is to count important terms.

exercises.explanation: Correct. Counting frequent normalized terms is useful for one report.
